turns.content: Alright, let me lay out the situation clearly. I'm a 31-year-old engineering geologist in Denver. I just ended a four-year relationship because my ex gave me an ultimatum: take a permanent desk job or no marriage. I refused—I've spent eight years building expertise in slope stability and core logging, and I'm not apologizing for field work. Starting soon, I'll be on a three-year contract with a brutal schedule: two weeks at an isolated mine site in northern Nevada, then two weeks off in Denver. I need a concrete, actionable plan for dating in those off-weeks—calendar structure, app strategy, maybe venues like climbing gyms or ceramic workshops. I want an efficient screening system to filter for people who genuinely respect an unconventional schedule. Can you help me build that framework?

Here's a framework built around your actual constraint: roughly 26 weeks/year of Denver availability, in fixed 14-day blocks, disclosed early.

## 1. Calendar structure

You get about 13 on-blocks per year. Treat each as a sprint:

- **Days 1–2 (Thu–Fri after return):** App swiping/messaging push, respond to backlog, set up first dates for days 3–7.
- **Days 3–9:** First dates. Cap at 3–4 per block; more than that and you're optimizing for volume over judgment.
- **Days 10–13:** Second dates with whoever passed screening, or rest — you need decompression time, and over-scheduling defeats that.
- **Day 14:** Fly out. Expect a natural conversation point here: "I leave tomorrow" is a real-world test of how they handle it.

A useful rhythm: aim for one first date per block rather than several. Consistent, low-volume dating over 13 blocks beats feast/famine.

## 2. App strategy

- **Hinge** is your best primary: prompts let you state the schedule in your profile, filtering before anyone matches you. Put it in a prompt plainly: *"I work 2 weeks on / 2 weeks off at a mine site in Nevada. It means half my year is fully free — and half I'm unreachable. That works great for the right person."*
- **Bumble** as secondary, same disclosure in bio.
- Skip Tinder — its user base skews toward casual availability expectations that clash with your model.
- **Field-time messaging:** keep apps active while at the site (assuming wifi). Two weeks of messaging is a natural low-cost screening phase before you ever spend an evening on someone. Someone who stays engaged over 14 days of text-only contact has already demonstrated tolerance for the schedule.

## 3. Screening system

Three filters, in order:

**Filter 1 — profile disclosure (passive):** Anyone who matches you has read the schedule. Ask in early chat: "How did the rotation thing land for you?" Their answer reveals a lot.

**Filter 2 — messaging (cheap, 1–2 weeks):** Look for: consistent response patterns without demanding instant replies; genuine questions about your work rather than glossing past it; their own full life (job, hobbies, friends). A person with a full independent life is structurally compatible with a 2/2 rotation. Red flag: resentment or testing behavior ("why didn't you text back faster") during a site block.

**Filter 3 — the rotation test (first 2–3 dates):** Watch how they handle the first departure after you've started dating. Someone who expresses mild disappointment but stays warm and makes plans for your return = compatible. Someone who goes cold, guilt-trips, or "checks out" = the filter worked.

Explicit first-date question worth asking directly: "Have you dated anyone with travel-heavy or rotation work before? How did that go?" Past behavior here is your best predictor.

## 4. Venues (Denver)

- **Climbing gyms:** Movement RiNo or Baker, Ubergrippen. Climbing attracts people comfortable with partners disappearing into the mountains/desert — demographically your best pool. Go at consistent times during off-blocks; regulars notice regulars.
- **Ceramics:** Yes — Colorado has a strong studio scene (e.g., community studios in RiNo/Westwood). Multi-week classes conflict with your rotation, though; book single-session workshops on days 3–10 instead of enrolling in 8-week courses.
- **Better fits than weekly classes:** weekend trail groups, one-off climbing clinics, trivia nights — anything drop-in rather than commitment-based.

## 5. One structural recommendation

You're optimizing for someone whose life doesn't require your daily presence but benefits from your full presence when home. Highest-probability matches: healthcare workers on shift schedules, teachers (summers), outdoor-industry workers, frequent-travel professionals, and people who explicitly value autonomy. Consider stating that preference in your screening conversations — it sharpens both directions of the filter.

**Tradeoff to acknowledge:** the 2/2 rotation delays the early-intimacy phase of any relationship by roughly 2x calendar time. Expect 6+ months of dating before someone has enough data to commit to the lifestyle long-term. Budget for that rather than treating it as failure.

One unknown worth checking before you start: whether your mine site has reliable wifi/cell. If not, your field-time messaging strategy changes — disclose the communication blackout explicitly in your profile instead.

I appreciate the thoroughness—you clearly put real thought into the calendar and the venue suggestions. But I've got to push back on your volume cap. I'm not aiming for a slow-burn, one-per-block approach. I want to schedule eight to ten first dates per 14-day off-cycle. I can sleep when I'm old. The numbers justify the grind—more shots on goal means better odds of finding someone who doesn't flinch at the rotation. Can we build a pipeline that actually supports that intensity rather than throttling it?

Your call to make — I'll flag the costs once, then build what you asked for.

**The honest tradeoff (one paragraph, then done):** 8–10 first dates in 14 days means roughly one per available day. The costs aren't sleep; they're (a) decision quality degrading under fatigue — you may misread people you'd read correctly fresh, (b) candidates becoming interchangeable in memory, which corrupts your screening data, and (c) some worthwhile people noticing they're one of many, especially if dates cluster at the same venues. Mitigations below address all three, but they don't eliminate them.

## The high-throughput pipeline

**Input volume math:** 8–10 dates requires roughly 15–20 solid conversations in progress, which requires roughly 30–50 quality matches per block. That input must be built *during* your on-rotation — the mine weeks become your sourcing phase, not downtime.

**During the 14 days on-site:**
- Swipe/message daily. This is where your funnel lives or dies.
- Run 15–25 parallel conversations. With that volume you need a system: a simple spreadsheet or notes app (name, app, 3 key facts, status, red flags noted). Without it, you *will* confuse details across people, and getting caught doing so ends candidates.
- Move promising conversations to a concrete plan *before* you land: "I'm back the 23rd through the 5th — want to grab a drink on the 25th?" Pre-booked dates fill the calendar; unbooked "let's meet up sometime" matches evaporate.
- Filter hard in chat so only genuine schedule-tolerant candidates get slots. At your volume you can't afford dates that fail Filter 2.

**During the 14 days off:**
- Stack short, low-cost first dates: coffee or one drink, 60–90 minutes, weekdays. Reserve dinner-length dates for second dates only.
- One per evening is sustainable; two per day (afternoon coffee + evening drink) is possible 2–3 times per block but is where decision quality drops fastest — cap doubles at that.
- Debrief immediately after each date: 3 bullet points in your notes app — schedule reaction, conversation quality, second-date yes/no. Do it same-night or the data blurs by day 5.
- Vary venues (2–3 rotation spots minimum) to avoid staff recognizing a pattern and to avoid date overlap.

**Rules that keep the filter functioning at volume:**
- The same-night written debrief is non-negotiable. At 10 dates, memory alone will merge candidates and your screening system becomes noise.
- Never double-book the same day with people from the same app who might know each other (climbing gym and ceramics scenes in Denver are small enough for this to happen).
- The rotation test still applies — but stagger departures' emotional weight by not front-loading the people you like most into the final 3 days before fly-out.

**Capacity check:** if your messaging pipeline yields fewer than ~8 bookable candidates, the constraint is sourcing, not scheduling — spend the off-block's downtime days on Hinge/Bumble input rather than lowering your filters to fill slots.

The throttle I suggested earlier was about data quality, not your stamina. With written debriefs and pre-booking from site, the 8–10 target is executable.

I get the system, but I'm still uneasy about something. You're right about the debrief notes—I'll do that. But the real bottleneck isn't calendar math, it's the disclosure question. Do I put the rotation in my profile or wait until the first date? My ex's ultimatum makes me paranoid that honesty just gives people an early reason to swipe left.

Put it in the profile. The reasoning follows from your own stated goal, not from a moral rule about honesty.

**The logic:** you defined the objective as filtering for people who don't flinch at the rotation. A person who swipes left on the schedule is a person your filter was designed to remove. Profile disclosure doesn't create that rejection — it moves it to a moment that costs you zero hours. Hiding it doesn't convert a flincher into a non-flincher; it converts the discovery into a sunk first date, possibly a second, and at your 8–10-per-block volume that's the actual bottleneck: every slot spent on someone who balks at week two is a slot a compatible person didn't get.

**On the paranoia specifically:** your evidence base for "disclosure backfires" is one data point — your ex. And note what actually happened there: she knew your work for four years and the conflict surfaced at the marriage decision, not at the start. That's not evidence that early disclosure fails. If anything it's evidence that *deferred* resolution of schedule incompatibility is the expensive path — four years expensive. You're generalizing a conclusion from a case that cuts the other way.

**The one real cost of profile disclosure:** it shrinks your top-of-funnel. Some people who *would* have been fine with the rotation in practice will swipe left on it in the abstract, because an unknown constraint reads worse on paper than it feels in a relationship. That's a genuine loss. But at your volume — 30–50 matches needed per block, sourced over 14 days of site-time swiping in a metro of 3 million — you can absorb a reduced match rate. The funnel math only breaks if you're in a small market. Denver isn't one.

**How to frame it so disclosure costs you the least:**
- State it as logistics plus upside, not as a warning. *"Two weeks on-site in Nevada, two weeks fully off in Denver. Means half my year I'm off the grid, half I'm completely free — long ski days, weeknight concerts, actual availability."* This is accurate (the 14 free days are real, consecutive, and more flexible than most 9–5 schedules) and it pre-loads the interpretation.
- Don't mention the ex, the ultimatum, or "looking for someone who accepts my job." Accept-frames signal a grievance you're asking strangers to adjudicate. State the schedule; let the filtering happen silently.
- Use the on-site messaging phase as the confirmation layer: people who matched knowing the schedule but start resenting slow replies during a rotation reveal it within one block, before you've spent an evening.

**When waiting would be defensible:** if you were dating casually without a long-term filter, delayed disclosure costs less. But that's not the system you asked me to build. For your stated pipeline, first-date disclosure is strictly the expensive version of the same information.

One caveat to hold loosely: if after 2–3 blocks your match rate is near zero, the profile framing is the variable to test — not the disclosure itself. A/B test the wording before concluding Denver can't support the funnel.

That's a clean argument, and I can't really find a flaw in it. My evidence base is one data point, and four-years-late rejection isn't the same as first-swipe rejection. I'll put it in the Hinge profile exactly as you framed it—logistics plus upside, no grievance. One last concern, though: do I say "off the grid" literally, or is that going to scare people more than the reality justifies? There's usually spotty satellite wifi at the site, not total silence.

Don't say "off the grid" — it's factually wrong for your situation, and the error costs you in both directions.

**Direction one:** as you suspected, it overshoots. "Off the grid" implies total unreachability, which screens out people who would be fine with "slow, sometimes patchy replies." You'd be filtering harder than your actual constraint requires.

**Direction two — the one that matters more:** it sets an expectation you then violate. If your profile says unreachable and you're texting from site wifi at 10pm, fine, that's a pleasant surprise. But the first time the satellite link drops for two days mid-conversation, someone who matched expecting "reachable but slow" experiences it as you going silent without warning — which reads as flakiness or loss of interest, not infrastructure failure. The people who interpret silence worst are often the ones you'd otherwise want to keep.

**Write the reality instead.** Something like: *"Two weeks at a mine site in Nevada — replies get slow and occasionally go dark for a day or two when the satellite link drops — then two weeks fully off in Denver."* This does three things at once: it's accurate, it pre-authorizes the gaps so a dead wifi day isn't interpreted as ghosting, and it keeps the upside framing intact.

**General rule worth applying throughout the profile and early dating:** describe the worst realistic version of the schedule, not the best and not a dramatized one. Underselling sets you up for the four-year-delayed rejection pattern; overselling (or over-dramatizing) filters out people your reality wouldn't have bothered. Precision is what makes your screening data trustworthy — candidates are consenting to the actual thing, so their reaction to it is real information.

Also add one behavioral safeguard for the gaps themselves: before each site rotation, tell active matches your return date. "Heading out tomorrow, back the 23rd" takes ten seconds and converts an ambiguous silence into a scheduled one. Ambiguity is what actually kills early-stage conversations, not the silence itself.

That's a good refinement—"replies get slow" instead of "off the grid." I'll use that phrasing. One more thing: I'm heading to the site in four days. Should I start swiping now from Denver to build a pipeline, or wait until I'm actually on-site so there's less time between match and first date?

Start now. The timing objection reverses itself once you look at your own funnel math.

**The gap you're worried about doesn't exist in your system.** Match now, message during the next four days, and the pre-booking step from the pipeline applies: anyone promising gets a concrete date offer for your first days back — roughly days 17–20 from now. Two to three weeks from match to first date is normal on apps, not a red flag. And matches who can't tolerate a defined three-week horizon with a named date attached are showing you schedule intolerance at zero cost — exactly what the filter exists to catch.

**What you get for the four days:**

1. **A debugging window in Denver.** You wrote the profile language this week and have never run it live. Starting now gives you four days of data on whether "replies get slow / satellite link" framing produces matches and how the disclosure question lands in early chat. If the match rate is weak or the profile reads wrong, you find out while you still have evenings free to rewrite — not from a cot in Nevada where the whole block's funnel depends on it.

2. **Your most credible messaging window.** Right now you can reply in real time. Candidates who engage well now, then stay warm when your replies slow on day five, have already passed a live version of the rotation test before you've spent a single evening. Starting from site means every new match meets you in degraded-communication mode from message one — first impressions formed at your worst response latency.

3. **Funnel head start.** You need ~15–25 conversations running to book 8–10 dates. Site-time is 14 days; adding 4 Denver days gives you 18 days of sourcing for your first block. Your first block is where the pipeline is least proven, so give it the most input.

**One sequencing note:** the days-one-and-two app push from your original calendar is now redundant for block one — you'll land with dates partially pre-booked. Use those days for rest and the debrief system setup instead. Rebuild the push into blocks two onward, when the pipeline runs purely on site-time sourcing.

Four days is short, but it's the only window you get to test the profile with full availability. Use it.
